title: NEB Class 11 Biology — Floral Diversity — 2022
subject: biology
source: NEB Grade 11 Model Questions / NEB Past Papers 2020-2024

questions.question: Describe the general characteristics of the phylum Bryophyta. Give two economic importance.
questions.solution:
**Characteristics:**
- Small, non-vascular plants (no true roots, stems, leaves)
- Dominant gametophyte generation
- Require water for fertilization
- Thalloid or leafy body
- Examples: Marchantia, Funaria

**Economic importance:**
1. Peat moss (Sphagnum) — fuel, packing material
2. Used as ornamental plants; some used in traditional medicine
questions.knowledgeNote: Bryophytes are 'amphibians of plant kingdom' — need water for reproduction.
questions.answer: **General characteristics of Bryophyta (the amphibians of the plant kingdom):** (1) **Non-vascular** — no true xylem/phloem; no true roots, stems or leaves (rhizoids anchor the thallus); small, growing in damp shady places; (2) **gametophyte dominant** — the green, photosynthetic plant is haploid; the sporophyte is short-lived and **dependent** on it; (3) **water needed for fertilisation** — motile biflagellate antherozoids swim to the archegonium (hence 'amphibians'); (4) reproduction via **archegonia (female) and antheridia (male)**; alternation of generations with a spore-producing sporophyte (capsule on a seta); e.g. *Marchantia*, moss (*Funaria*). **Two economic importances:** (1) **peat/moss uses** — *Sphagnum* peat as fuel and as packing material for transporting live plants (high water-holding); (2) **soil formation and prevention of erosion** — bryophytes colonise bare rock, build soil, and retain moisture in forests (also used as beddings, antiseptic dressing in *Sphagnum*). **Deep point:** the water-dependent fertilisation is the group's defining constraint — it confines bryophytes to damp habitats and explains why they never conquered dry land the way vascular plants did.

questions.question: Differentiate between dicotyledonous and monocotyledonous angiosperms with one example of each.
questions.solution:
Angiosperms are divided into **Dicotyledonae (dicots)** and **Monocotyledonae (monocots)**:

| Feature | Dicotyledonae (dicots) | Monocotyledonae (monocots) |
|---|---|---|
| **Cotyledons** | **Two** cotyledons in the seed | **One** cotyledon (the scutellum) |
| **Leaf venation** | **Reticulate (net-like)** | **Parallel** |
| **Root system** | **Tap root** bearing lateral roots; shows secondary growth | **Fibrous/adventitious** root system; no secondary growth |
| **Stem** | Vascular bundles arranged in a **ring**; has vascular cambium and shows secondary growth | Vascular bundles **scattered** in the ground tissue; no cambium |
| **Flower** | Parts in **fours or fives** — 5 sepals, 5 petals, 5 stamens, 2 carpels | Parts in **threes or multiples of three** — 5 sepals absent, usually 3+3 per whorl |
| **Stomata** | Present on **both** surfaces of the leaf | Present mostly on the **lower** surface only |
| **Pollen grains** | **Tricolpate** (three colpi) | **Monocolpate** (one colpus) |
| **Examples** | Potato (*Solanum tuberosum*), tomato, pea (*Pisum*), mustard (*Brassica*) | Onion (*Allium cepa*), maize (*Zea mays*), rice, wheat, sugarcane |

**Conclusion:** Dicots have two cotyledons, reticulate venation and a ring of vascular bundles, whereas monocots have one cotyledon, parallel venation and scattered vascular bundles.
questions.knowledgeNote: Dicots have two cotyledons, reticulate venation and a tap root; monocots have one cotyledon, parallel venation and fibrous roots.
questions.answer: **Dicotyledonous vs monocotyledonous angiosperms:** **Seed:** dicots have **two cotyledons** in the embryo; monocots have **one**. **Leaf venation:** dicots — **reticulate (net-like)**; monocots — **parallel**. **Root system:** dicots — **tap root**; monocots — **fibrous (adventitious) root**. **Floral parts:** dicots in **fours or fives** (or multiples); monocots in **threes** (or multiples of three). **Vascular bundles in the stem:** dicots — **ringed, open (cambium present)**; monocots — **scattered, closed (no cambium)**. **Examples:** dicot — **mango, mustard, bean, pea**; monocot — **maize, wheat, rice, onion, banana**. **Deep point:** one seed-leaf count predicts the leaf, root, flower and stem pattern — the cotyledon number is the cheapest diagnostic in botany.
